# Voiceverse NFT plagiarism scandal

The **Voiceverse NFT plagiarism scandal** was a significant controversy in January 2022 concerning the discovery that Voiceverse, an NFT company backed by the Bored Ape Yacht Club and voice actor Troy Baker, had plagiarized voice content from 15.ai, a non-commercial text-to-speech service . The scandal highlighted ethical issues in the emerging AI voice technology and NFT markets, involving unauthorized use of AI-generated content, false marketing claims, and subsequent public backlash .

## Background

### 15.ai and its creator

15.ai was a free, non-commercial text-to-speech service created by a pseudonymous MIT researcher known as "15" . The service, launched in March 2020, allowed users to generate voice samples from various fictional characters including those from My Little Pony, Portal, Team Fortress 2, and Doctor Who . The creator had explicitly stated in December 2021 that they had "no interest in incorporating NFTs into any aspect of \[their] work" .

The service utilized a technology called DeepThroat, which was capable of voice cloning with minimal data . 15.ai was developed using a combination of audio synthesis algorithms, speech synthesis deep neural networks, and sentiment analysis . The project began development while the creator was an undergraduate at MIT and had been in development for years before its public release .

### Voiceverse and its concept

Voiceverse was a startup founded by the Bored Ape Yacht Club (BAYC), one of the most prominent NFT collections at the time . The company's concept was to create a platform where users could purchase voice IP rights as NFTs using cryptocurrency . The idea was to allow users to buy the rights to a particular voice - originally performed by a voice actor - as an NFT, which could then be used to create AI-powered voice lines .

The company's founders included those who later created Lovo, a voice technology company . On their pitch website, they stated their vision: "A person's voice is uniquely linked to their identity" .

## Timeline of events

### January 14, 2022: Initial announcement

On January 14, 2022, voice actor Troy Baker announced his partnership with Voiceverse NFT via Twitter . In his announcement, Baker stated that the partnership would "explore ways where together we might bring new tools to new creators to make new things, and allow everyone a chance to own & invest in the IP's they create" .

Anticipating potential criticism, Baker added a controversial statement: "We all have a story to tell. You can hate. Or you can create. What'll it be?" . This immediately triggered backlash from fans and the gaming community, with concerns that AI voice technology could displace human voice actors and enable fraud .

### Within hours: First accusations

Just nine hours after Baker's initial announcement, he began walking back some of his statements . He described his tone as "a bit antagonistic," stating he was "just a storyteller out here trying to tell my story to whomever will hear..." .

Later that same day, 15, the creator of 15.ai, alleged that Voiceverse had used their service to create a promotional video . Through server log screenshots, 15 revealed that Voiceverse had generated voice lines using the 15.ai platform, pitch-shifted the audio to make it unrecognizable, and falsely marketed the samples as their own technology before selling them as NFTs .

Specifically, 15.ai accused Voiceverse of using their service to create a voice for a cartoon character from the "Chubbiverse" NFT collection . The creator stated: "Unbelievable. They even pitched up the voice to intentionally make it sound unrecognizable from Rainbow Dash's original voice," referring to a My Little Pony character available on the 15.ai service .

### January 15, 2022: Apology and response

Initially, Voiceverse denied any wrongdoing . However, within an hour of being confronted with evidence, Voiceverse issued an apology . In their tweet to 15.ai, they wrote: "Hey @fifteenai we are extremely sorry about this. The voice was indeed taken from your platform, which our marketing team used without giving proper credit. Chubbiverse team has no knowledge of this. We will make sure this never happens again" .

15.ai's response was brief and direct: "Go fuck yourself" .

### January 31, 2022: Baker ends partnership

After over two weeks of 持续 criticism, Troy Baker announced on January 31, 2022, that he would end his partnership with Voiceverse NFT . In his apology tweet, Baker stated: "Thank you all for your feedback and patience. After careful consideration, I've decided to not continue the partnership with Voiceverse NFT. Intentions aside, I've heard you and apologize for accusing anyone of 'hating' just by simply disagreeing with me" .

## Impact and aftermath

### Immediate consequences

The scandal had significant immediate consequences for all parties involved. Voiceverse's reputation was severely damaged, with the company largely "fizzling out" following the controversy . The incident highlighted the unethical practices in the NFT and AI voice technology space, particularly the unauthorized use of non-commercial AI-generated content for profit .

The scandal also had broader implications for the voice acting industry, with many voice actors expressing concern about the potential misuse of their voices through AI technology . The incident was noted as the first instance of speech synthesis NFT plagiarism and fraud .

### Long-term developments

In May 2024, Lovo, Voiceverse's parent company, was sued by a group of voice actors in a class action lawsuit . The lawsuit alleged that Lovo had stolen voices and identities of voice actors to create millions of voice-over productions without permission or proper compensation, violating numerous state right of privacy laws and the federal Lanham Act .

The lawsuit specifically mentioned Voiceverse, stating that "the founders of Lovo even created another company, Voiceverse, which sold voice NFTs" . The plaintiffs alleged that Lovo had misrepresented the use of voice recordings, telling voice actors that their voices would be used only for academic research purposes .

In July 2024, the judge allowed the claims to move forward , indicating that the legal repercussions of the Voiceverse scandal were still being felt years after the initial incident.

## Notable reactions

### From the voice acting community

The Voiceverse scandal sparked widespread discussion within the voice acting community. Many voice actors criticized the NFT partnership, with particular concern about the fact that voice actors could only receive royalties when voice NFTs were sold . The incident raised awareness about the potential exploitation of voice actors through AI technology and NFTs.

### From the technology community

The scandal was also notable for being one of the early cases of AI-generated content plagiarism between AI systems . As noted in a retrospective analysis: "It's strange to think that, in January 2022, we had a plagiarism controversy not over whether a work was AI or human-created, but about which AI system created it" .

The incident highlighted the growing issue of AI systems potentially plagiarizing each other, which has become more relevant with the increasing sophistication of AI technology .

### Media coverage

The scandal received significant media coverage, with articles appearing in major gaming and technology publications including Eurogamer, Stevivor, Tech Times, and others . The coverage helped bring attention to the ethical issues surrounding AI voice technology and NFTs, contributing to broader discussions about the regulation of these emerging technologies.

## Legacy

The Voiceverse NFT plagiarism scandal is remembered as a pivotal moment in the development of AI voice technology and the NFT market. It served as a cautionary tale about the unethical use of AI-generated content and the potential for exploitation within the NFT ecosystem .

The scandal also highlighted the need for clearer regulations and ethical guidelines in the AI voice technology space, particularly regarding the use of non-commercial AI services for commercial purposes. As noted in a 2025 retrospective: "If this scandal had happened in 2025, things would have gone very differently. The focus would have been on the commercial AI company using the work of a free, solo-developed project to do what it should have been able to do easily" .

The case has been referenced in discussions about AI plagiarism more broadly, with commentators noting that it "may be predicting a future in which AI companies are suddenly very interested in who has permission to do what" . The Voiceverse scandal thus stands as an important early example of the ethical challenges facing the AI and NFT industries as they continue to develop and intersect.

Troy Baker-backed NFT company admits to using content without permission
========================================================================

18 Jan 2022

[Steve Wright](https://stevivor.com/author/stevivor/)

"Go f*ck yourself," replies 15.ai, the service that was wronged by Voiceverse NFT.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Voiceverse NFT, a [Troy Baker](https://stevivor.com/tag/troy-baker/)-backed non-fungible token (NFT) company, has admitted to using content without permission from 15.ai, a non-commercial text-to-speech service.

15.ai is a service that allows users to create an artificial voice by sampling recordings; as an example, you could upload samples from Patrick Stewart as Captain Jean-Luc Picard and then have ‘Picard’ say whatever you input. Voiceverse NFT has admitted to using the service to generate a sample that could theoretically have be sold on as an NFT.

The creator of 15.ai [took to Twitter](https://twitter.com/fifteenai/status/1482055102919757835) over the weekend and advised they were aware that Voiceverse NFT was “actively attempting to appropriate my work for their own benefit.”

Voiceverse NFT responded to the claim by boasting sarcastically; the tweet in question [has since been deleted](https://twitter.com/fifteenai/status/1482059305360797702) and replaced with an apology.

“We are extremely sorry about this,” the [replacement tweet](https://twitter.com/VoiceverseNFT/status/1482067251704434688) reads. “The voice was indeed taken from your platform, which our marketing team used without giving proper credit. Chubbiverse team has no knowledge of this. We will make sure this never happens again.”

The creator of 15.ai [responded](https://twitter.com/fifteenai/status/1482088782765576192), simply: “Go fuck yourself.” Back in December of last year, the creator [stated](https://twitter.com/fifteenai/status/1470190153188749313) “I have no interest in incorporating NFTs into any aspect of my work. Please stop asking.”

Baker — the voice behind _The Last of Us_‘ Joel, _Batman Arkham Origins_‘ Batman and many more characters — took to Twitter last week to promote Voiceverse NFT.

“We all have a story to tell,” [Baker wrot](https://twitter.com/TroyBakerVA/status/1481869350621437955)e as part of an imflammatory tweet.

“You can hate. Or you can create.”

In follow-up tweets, [Baker has admitted](https://twitter.com/TroyBakerVA/status/1482010647726460930) that “the ‘hate/create’ part might have been a bit antagonistic” but has not spoken to Voiceverse NFT’s sampling as yet. At the time of writing, Baker is still associated with the company.

UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT 

SOUTHERN DISTRICT OF NEW YORK 

PAUL LEHRMAN and LINNEA SAGE, on 

behalf of themselves and all others similarly 

situated, 

Plaintiffs, 

v. 

LOVO, INC., 

Defendant. 

No. 

CLASS ACTION 

DEMAND FOR JURY TRIAL 

CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT 

Plaintiffs Paul Lehrman and Linnea Sage (“Plaintiffs”), on behalf of themselves 

and all others similarly situated, for their Complaint against Defendant Lovo, Inc. 

(“LOVO”), state as follows: 

NATURE OF THE ACTION 

1. This is a class action brought on behalf of Plaintiffs and similarly situated 

persons whose voices and/or identities were stolen and used by LOVO – to create 

millions of voice -over productions – without permission or proper compensation, in 

violation of numerous state right of privacy laws, and the federal Lanham Act. LOVO is 

a technology company with proprietary software driven by artificial intelligence (AI) 

that allows LOVO’s clients to create and edit voice -over narration s adapted from real 

actors. To b e clear, the product that customers purchase from LOVO is stolen property. 

They are voices stolen by LOVO and marketed by LOVO under false pretenses: LOVO 

represents that it has the legal right to market these voices, but it does not. 

# Case 1:24-cv-03770 Document 1 Filed 05/16/24 Page 1 of 37 - 2 -

THE PARTIES 

2. Plaintiff Paul Lehrman is a resident of New York and is a voice -over 

actor. 

3. Plaintiff Linnea Sage is a resident of New York a nd is a voice -over actor. 

4. Defendant Lovo, Inc. is a Delaware -incorporated corporation with a 

principal address of 2150 Shattuck Avenue, Berkeley, California 94704 .

JURISDICTION AND VENUE 

5. This Court has subject matter jurisdiction pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1331 

because this action arises under the laws of the United States; and under 28 U.S.C. 

§ 1332 because the matter in controversy exceeds the sum or value of $75,000, exclusive 

of interest and costs, and is between citizens of different states. 

6. This Court has personal jurisdiction over Defendant because Defendant 

regularly conducts business in New York County. 

7. In addition, under 28 U.S.C. § 1367, this Court may exercise 

supplemental jurisdiction over the state law claims because all claims are derived from 

a common nucleus of operative facts and are such that Plaintiffs would ordinarily 

expect to try them in one judicial proceeding. 

8. In addition, under 28 U.S.C. § 1332(d)(2) , this Court shall have original 

jurisdiction of any civil action in which the matter in controversy exceeds the sum or 

value of $5,000,000, exclusive of interest and costs, and is a class action in which any 

member of a class of plaintiffs is a citizen of a State different from any defendant 

(28 U.S.C. § 1332(d)(2) (A) ).

9. Venue is proper in this Court under 28 U.S.C. § 1391(b) (2) because a 

substantial part of the events and omissions that give rise to the claims alleged herein 

# Case 1:24-cv-03770 Document 1 Filed 05/16/24 Page 2 of 37 - 3 -

occurred in New York County, the principal injuries stemming from the violations 

alleged herein occurred in the State of New York, and this Court has personal 

jurisdiction over Defendant. 

BACKGROUND 

10. The voice -over industry is estimated to generate more than $2 billion 

annually in the United States, and more than $4 billion annually worldwide. 

11. Voice -overs, commonly known as narrations, are integral to various 

industries, spanning entertainment, advertising, marketing, education, and other 

corporate sectors. They serve as indispensable tools across a wide array of mediums, 

including film and tele vision, commercials, animation, audiobooks, e -learning, 

corporate presentations, marketing presentations, educational videos, interactive voice 

response (IVR) systems, podcasting, video games, documentaries, virtual assistants, 

public announcements, dubbin g, radio imaging, audio dramas, museum exhibits, phone 

systems, language learning, medical narration, corporate training modules, websites, 

sales pitches, and digital content. They are even used in venture capital funding 

pitches. 

12. Traditionally, actors are hired to read scripts, which may be recorded in 

outside studios or with the actor’s own equipment. The recordings are then edited, 

changes or re -recordings produced, and a final recording is laid into the show or 

presentation. 

13. The actors are paid a negotiated amount for the use of their voices, and 

typically for the time spent recording the audio requested. The negotiated amount is a 

function of the actor’s name, brand value, where , and in what medium the voice -over 

will be used, and for how long it will be used. Payments typically include upfront fees, 

# Case 1:24-cv-03770 Document 1 Filed 05/16/24 Page 3 of 37 - 4 -

royalties, residuals , or some combination of these payments . And there are other 

potential fees required under Screen Actors Guild – American Federation of Television 

and Radio Artists (SAG -AFTRA) contracts. 

14. Actors like Plaintiffs get paid anywhere from $150 for a short recording 

for a local television tag, to $2,000 for a one -time sales presentation, to $6,000 

minimum for a 13 -week run of a TV commercial , or more depending on the project .1

Established actors can typically make much more via residuals, and through daily fees 

which can exceed $1,000 per day and can involve several weeks of work. 

15. Failure to pay the actor a negotiated and agreed -upon price for their 

professional services – and often recognizable voice – is a violation of multiple statutes 

and common law. 

16. Defendant LOVO, by its own admission, is attempting to disrupt and 

“revolutionize” this traditional model. LOVO sells a text -to -speech subscription service 

that allows its clients – typically companies – to generate voice -over narrations at a 

fraction of the cost of the traditional model. LOVO does this by allowing subscribing 

customers to upload a script into its AI -driven software known as “Generator” or 

“Genny ,” and generate a professional -quality voice -over based on certain criteria. For 

example, LOVO c ustomers can choose between – and designate their preference for –

male or female voices, regional accents, and older or younger -sounding voices.  

> 1

See, e.g. , Global Voice Acting Academy, GVAA Rate Guide, 

https://globalvoiceacademy.com/gvaa -rate -guide -2/ .

# Case 1:24-cv-03770 Document 1 Filed 05/16/24 Page 4 of 37 - 5 -

17. As of January 2023, LOVO had created over 7 million voice -overs. 2 In a 

podcast, LOVO’s chief executive officer and co -founder Tom Lee explained how LOVO’s 

synthetic speech platform works: 

[I]magine … you have a real human voice, and we take that, and 

clone that, and make it available as an option for you to turn any 

text that you have into that voice. So, you can make that voice say 

anything that you want, even if that person has never actu ally said 

that before in their life. 

18. In that same 2023 podcast, Mr. Lee then stated that LOVO “ only need[s] a 

person to read 50 sentences. … We can capture the tone, the character, the style, the 

phonemes, and if you have an accent, we can even capture that as well.” 

19. LOVO also promotes its service using barely -disguised images and names 

of celebrities and states on its website, “Clone any voice .” Only deep in its website does 

LOVO tell customers , “Mind you, you cannot use this cloned voice for imitation of 

celebrities, so only use this tool for personal entertainment purposes!” 

20. LOVO purports to compensate voice actors. That may be true in some 

cases. But Plaintiffs and other members of the class have received no revenue from the 

continued unauthorized use of their voices by LOVO and LOVO clients. 

21. The benefit to the business subscriber of using LOVO’s service is 

financial: they do not have to pay the actor the studio session, any residuals, royalties, 

or fees – beyond the monthly subscription cost paid to LOVO. 

22. Implicit in LOVO’s offerings to its customers is that each voice -over actor 

has agreed to LOVO’s terms and conditions for customers to be able to access that  

> 2

Category Visionaries , Podcast, “Tom Lee, Co -Founder of LOVO AI: $7 Million Raised 

to Build the Future of AI Voiceovers” (Jan. 2023). 

# Case 1:24-cv-03770 Document 1 Filed 05/16/24 Page 5 of 37 - 6 -

actor’s voice. But for Plaintiffs and other members of the class who have not agreed to 

LOVO’s terms, the continued unauthorized use of Plaintiffs’ voices is theft of service 

and misappropriation. 

23. Plaintiff s and many members of the class are members of SAG -AFTRA. 

24. On its website, LOVO represents to potential clients that it has 

agreements with actors allowing LOVO to utilize those actors’ voices and compensating 

them appropriately for that use. That may be true with respect to some actors, but it is 

emphatically not true with respect to Plaintiffs : LOVO had no permission to use 

Plaintiffs’ voices for training its AI Generator, to promote the LOVO service, or to 

market voices based on Plaintiffs’ voices. And LOVO never compensated Plaintiffs for 

any of LOVO’s unauthorized uses of Pla intiffs’ voices. 

25. Upon information and belief, LOVO has not entered into any agreement 

with SAG -AFTRA pertaining to the employment of its members for voice -over services. 

Those agreements are designed to protect the rights of SAG -AFTRA members – like 

Plaintiffs Sage and Lehrman –who are required by SAG -AFTRA’s Global Rule 1 to 

eschew jobs that are not covered by the union’s contract. By bypassing or ignoring the 

terms of agreements between SAG -AFTRA and producers and/or companies that are 

signatories to SAG -AFTRA agreements, LOVO endangers Plaintiffs’ livelihood. Using 

Plaintiffs’ voices without their consent may pu t Plaintiffs in involuntary breach of their 

union obligations and contracts. 

26. LOVO represents to its customers that LOVO is granting to the customer 

full commercial rights for all content generated using its platform to users who 

subscribe to any of its paid plans (Basic, Pro, Pro+, and Enterprise). Yet LOVO does not 

# Case 1:24-cv-03770 Document 1 Filed 05/16/24 Page 6 of 37 - 7 -

legally own or control the rights it is purporting to give these customers – rights which 

remain with the actors whose voices have been illegally cloned or otherwise 

misappropriated. 

27. Indeed, any cost -avoidance completely depends upon the actor agreeing to 

participate in LOVO’s scheme. Plaintiffs did not agree to LOVO’s terms and did not 

grant LOVO any right to market their voices. In fact, Plaintiffs specifically rejected all 

entreaties to participate in an y AI -driven voice -related software . Moreover, LOVO 

affirmatively misrepresented how Plaintiffs’ voices would be used. And yet, LOVO used 

its proprietary software to appropriate, adapt, generate, steal, and market Plaintiffs’ 

voices. 

DEFENDANT’S MISAPPROPRIATION OF PLAINTIFFS’ VOICES 

Plaintiff Lehrman 

28. In May 2020 Mr. Lehrman was contacted via the Fiverr website to provide 

voice -over narrative services .

29. Fiverr.com is an online marketplace that connects freelancers with clients 

looking for digital and creative services. 

30. Using the Fiverr platform, Mr. Lehrman communicated about the inquiry 

with someone who can now only be identified as “User25199087” (because the account 

has since been deleted). 

31. As Mr. Lehrman was preparing to upload the voice files requested by the 

hiring company, on May 12, 2020 , he asked User25199087, “In addition can you please 

explain how the voiceovers will be used?” 

# Case 1:24-cv-03770 Document 1 Filed 05/16/24 Page 7 of 37 - 8 -

32. At 9:24 PM on May 12, 2020, User25199087 sent Mr. Lehrman a message: 

“We are researching speech synthesis with different accents and voices. Your voiceover 

will be used for academic research purposes only.” 

33. Mr. Lehrman wrote back to User25199087, “Great. Still working through 

the scripts. Please guarantee that these scripts will not be used for anything other than 

your specific research project. My curiosity is getting the best of me. What is the goal of 

the research project?” 

34. User25199087 wrote back to Mr. Lehrman, “The scripts will not be used 

for anything else - and I can’t yet tell you the goal, as it’s a confidential work in process 

sorry haha.” 

35. Mr. Lehrman responded to User25199087, “That’s okay. Will my voice be 

repurposed and used in a different order?” 

36. To which User25199087 wrote to Mr. Lehrman, “The script and your 

finished file will be used for research purposes only.” 

37. Mr. Lehrman delivered the requested voice files via Fiverr and was paid 

$1,200. 

38. In 2020, at the time of the online communications between Mr. Lehrman 

and User25199087, neither Mr. Lehrman, most other class plaintiffs, nor the general 

public had any idea what “speech synthesis” was. That Mr. Lehrman’s voice was being 

used “for academic research purposes only” was a reasonable explanation. At no time 

did User25199087 ever accurately represent that Mr. Lehrman’s voice would be used 

for anything other than “academic research purposes” – certainly not for commercial 

purposes. 

# Case 1:24-cv-03770 Document 1 Filed 05/16/24 Page 8 of 37 - 9 -

39. Several years later, Mr. Lehrman learned that User25199087 was an 

employee of Defendant LOVO, and the company that reach ed out to and hired Mr. 

Lehrman was LOVO. 

40. On March 28, 2022, Mr. Lehrman was approached by Fiverr and asked if 

he would like to add an AI software option to his Fiverr profile. Mr. Lehrman was told 

by the Fiverr executive that the AI software option would integrate software to his 

profile and allow customers to hear what Mr. Lehrman’s voice could sound like if he 

were to read a script. 

41. Mr. Lehrman declined the invitation to add that AI/software to his Fiverr 

profile. 

42. Mr. Lehrman demonstrated to Fiverr that a user could easily produce 

commercial audio without consent or compensation as well as create violent, 

pornographic, or any unauthorized audio material without consent from the voice 

actor. 

43. On or about April 6, 2022, Plaintiffs learned that iNTECH, a YouTube 

channel (now called Military News) with more than 336,000 subscribers, had created 

and was promoting videos about Russian military equipment that used Plaintiff 

Lehrman’s AI -generated voice. To be clear: Mr. Lehrman never recorded the YouTube 

video s; they were generated by a then -unidentified AI software without Mr. Lehrman’s 

participation or approval. 

44. Concerned about the unauthorized replication of his voice on the YouTube 

channel, Mr. Lehrman contacted the Fiverr executive who had approached him on 

March 28, 2022, seeking help to identify the AI software used. The Fiverr executive

2.title: A Retrospective on the Voiceverse Plagiarism Scandal
2.description: In January 2022, the NFT platform Voiceverse was at the center of an embarrassing plagiarism scandal. Years later, it was clearly a warning of what was to come.
2.content:
![Image 1: VoiceVerse Logo](https://www.plagiarismtoday.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/1637656002144.jpeg.webp)

January 2022 was a bizarre time. The COVID-19 lockdowns were ending, and life was returning to its new normal. We were, almost universally, in a period of transition.

The internet was in a very similar place. We were still 10 months away from the public launch of ChatGPT, but the heady days of NFTs were (largely) behind us. Though AI was definitely a buzzword, NFTs were still the internet pariah of the moment, raising concerns about environmental impact, fraud and a myriad of other issues.

So it’s appropriate that, during that month, a plagiarism scandal would arise that combined the two elements.

That’s precisely what the Voiceverse plagiarism scandal did.

To make matters even more impressive, Voiceverse was backed by one of the best-known NFT groups, which persuaded one of the most famous video game voice actors to participate.

This made it not just a significant story for NFT and AI fans, but also for the general public. It “broke containment” in a way few niche plagiarism scandals do.

As such, it’s worth looking back at this story, including what happened and what it can tell us about the future.

#### **Understanding the Voiceverse Plagiarism Scandal**

Voiceverse was (and as of this writing still is) a startup founded by the Bored Ape Yacht Club, one of the most famous NFT collections. The idea is simple: using a short audio sample, you can create a custom text-to-speech voice that you can own as an NFT and license others to use.

The idea was always going to be controversial, especially since there was no way to verify that the user owned the voice they were using.

However, [that controversy escalated further when](https://www.eurogamer.net/video-game-voice-actor-troy-baker-is-now-promoting-nfts), on January 14, 2022, video game voice actor [Troy Baker announced that he was partnering with Voiceverse](https://x.com/TroyBakerVA/status/1481869350621437955) to “bring new tools to new creators to make new things, and allow everyone a chance to own & invest in the IPs they create.”

Just nine hours later, Baker was walking some of that back. He described his tone as “a bit antagonistic,” and he is “just a storyteller out here trying to tell my story to whomever will hear…”

While that would have been bad enough, things quickly went from bad to worse for Voiceverse.

Fifteen, the pseudonymous creator of 15.ai, alleged that the Voiceverse promotion video was made using their system. They alleged that Voiceverse further altered the speech in a bid to make it unrecognizable.

Fifteen launched 15.ai in 2020, offering a simple, non-commercial tool for converting text to speech. Currently, you can use 15.ai to generate short voice samples using various _My Little Pony_ characters.

Initially, [Voiceverse denied any copying](https://www.eurogamer.net/troy-baker-backed-nft-firm-admits-using-voice-lines-taken-from-another-service-without-permission), but later apologized, saying that their “marketing team” had used it without proper credit.

Fifteen’s response was simply, “Go fuck yourself.”

Fifteen’s work has been widely credited for [paving the way for modern voice AI systems](https://independent.ng/the-mit-project-that-paved-way-for-modern-voice-ai/). However, Fifteen itself has been very adamant that its service is non-commercial, including NFTs.

This made Voiceverse’s use not just an act of plagiarism, but an affront to Fifteen’s stated beliefs.

Voiceverse has largely fizzled out following the scandal. However, in May 2024, Voiceverse’s parent company, Lovo, [was sued by a group of voice actors](https://www.reuters.com/legal/ai-voiceover-company-stole-voices-actors-new-york-lawsuit-claims-2024-05-16/). That case is ongoing, [with the judge allowing the claims to move forward in July of this year](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cedgzj8z1wjo).

However, that still leaves many interesting questions about Voiceverse’s misuse of 15.ai.

#### **When AI Plagiarizes AI**

Four years after the Voiceverse plagiarism scandal, we would have a strangely similar war of words, this time with much larger players.

The Chinese company [DeepSeek released its R1 and V3 models](https://www.plagiarismtoday.com/2025/01/28/how-deepseek-may-change-ai-copyright-and-plagiarism/). These models briefly shook the AI landscape, delivering results comparable to those of US-based companies at a fraction of the cost.

However, [OpenAI accused DeepSeek of “distilling” their models](https://www.plagiarismtoday.com/2025/01/29/the-schadenfreude-of-openai-attacking-deepseek/). However, as others point out, “distilling” is precisely what AIs do to human works to create their models in the first place. As such, much of the response to OpenAI’s allegations was more shadenfruede than sympathetic.

But Fifteen’s story was different for several reasons. First, AI was still much newer and had not become the focus of so much vitriol. Second, Fifteen is a solo developer who has insisted that their work is to be used only for non-commercial purposes. Finally, Voiceverse didn’t simply distil his model; they used the 15.ai service directly. They did no original work in this process.

Still, it’s strange to think that, in January 2022, we had a plagiarism controversy not over whether a work was AI or human-created, but about which AI system created it.

While this may be one of the first such stories, it will definitely not be the last. The DeepSeek story showed us that AI companies, at least theoretically, can take shortcuts using each other’s work. In a race as cutthroat as the AI one, any shortcut that can be exploited likely will.

The growing question isn’t whether humans are using AI systems to plagiarize or even if AIs are plagiarizing humans. It’s whether they are plagiarizing each other.

That is a growing problem that we have only seen the very beginnings of.

#### **Bottom Line**

If this scandal had happened in 2025, things would have gone very differently. The focus would have been on the commercial AI company using the work of a free, solo-developed project to do what it should have been able to do easily.

If you’re going to purport to allow users to generate thousands of voices, you should at least be able to develop the one voice in your promotion video. That seems obvious. Voiceverse didn’t just plagiarize; it failed at the most basic task it was supposed to do.

But imagine if this hadn’t been a solo developer. Instead, [they had used OpenAI or a similar service](https://openai.com/index/introducing-our-next-generation-audio-models/). There would almost certainly have been a lawsuit and technical measures put in place. To prevent future misuse.

But that is a story that I’ve seen over and over again these past 20 years. Many people dismiss copyright and/or plagiarism issues until it is their work that is taken. We’re seeing that with AI companies, too. These companies defend their right to train on whatever human-created content they want, but become upset when their work is misused.

While I don’t put Fifteen in the same category as OpenAI for a myriad of reasons, this case was still an interesting preview of what was and still is to come.

[We already know that AI is being trained on AI-generated content](https://www.technologyreview.com/2024/07/24/1095263/ai-that-feeds-on-a-diet-of-ai-garbage-ends-up-spitting-out-nonsense/), much to its detriment. What happens when AI companies use competitors’ creations to fake their capabilities? Has it already happened? The black box nature of AI makes it difficult to know.

While the Voiceverse case may get lumped in with the other NFT scandals of that time, it’s the AI component that makes it more relevant. In that regard, it may be predicting a future in which AI companies are suddenly very interested in who has permission to do what.

However, that doesn’t mean they’ll care about what human creators think, just other AI companies.

6.title: Troy Baker Apologizes for NFT Tweet and Calling Critics ‘Haters’
6.description: Troy Baker apologizes for the controversy surrounding his NFT Twitter post, and saying people should "create," not "hate."
6.content:
Troy Baker has apologized for a controversial Twitter post in which he announced a partnership with an NFT company, [before being dismissive of critics of non-fungible tokens.](https://www.playstationlifestyle.net/2022/01/14/troy-baker-nfts-hate-or-create/)_The Last of Us_ voice actor has said that he will now no longer work with VoiceverseNFT after “careful consideration.”

Troy Baker NFT Twitter controversy explained
--------------------------------------------

Voice actor Baker, who is most known for his work as Joel in Naughty Dog’s _The Last of Us_ and its sequel, previously tweeted his support for VoiceVerseNFT, a company that ostensibly allows users to purchase ‘Voice NFTs’ that they can theoretically use in different games.

Baker tweeted that the platform would “allow everyone a chance to own and invest in the IPs they create,” before concluding: “You can hate. Or you can create. What’ll it be?”

With NFTs being roundly criticized for the environmental damage they cause, and VoiceverseNFT specifically coming under fire for using [voice lines from another service](https://www.eurogamer.net/articles/2022-01-17-troy-baker-backed-nft-firm-admits-using-voice-lines-taken-from-another-service-without-permission) without permission, Troy has now stepped away from his partnership with the program.

In a tweet, Baker said that “intentions aside” he had heard his critics and apologized for accusing them of “hating” by disagreeing with him:

> Thank you all for your feedback and patience. After careful consideration, I’ve decided to not continue the partnership with VoiceVerseNFT. Intentions aside, I’ve heard you and apologize for accusing anyone of “hating” just by simply disagreeing with me.
> 
> 
> — Troy Baker (@TroyBakerVA) [January 31, 2022](https://twitter.com/TroyBakerVA/status/1488151018726510594?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw)

Voiceverse NFT responded to Troy Baker’s comment, saying that it had “mutually decided” to end the partnership with the voice actor. Additionally, Voiceverse said it would “double-down” and its resources to execute its roadmap and strengthen its community along with the “broader NFT ecosystem.”

> We have mutually decided to end our partnership with Troy Baker, and will double-down our resources and efforts to execute on our roadmap, further our vision as the voice of Web3.0, and strengthen our community as well as the broader NFT ecosystem.
> 
> 
> — Voiceverse ? (@TheVoiceverse) [January 31, 2022](https://twitter.com/TheVoiceverse/status/1488150076795011073?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw)

Baker’s comments were widely criticized after he posted the initial tweet, with many accusing him of being condescending by seemingly labeling all critics of NFTs as simply looking to “hate” the technology.

Shortly after the tweet went viral for all the wrong reasons, Baker appeared on the podcast Play, Watch, Listen alongside Santa Monica Studio’s Alanah Pearce and _Thomas Was Alone_ creator Mike Bithell— who are both opposed to NFTs— where they discussed the fallout to the tweet and how his intention was to instead be “inspiring” about the platform.

[![Image 1: YouTube video player](https://i.ytimg.com/vi/HcJDYkm4jZA/hqdefault.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HcJDYkm4jZA)

In other news, a [PS5 version of](https://www.playstationlifestyle.net/2022/01/31/cyberpunk-2077-ps5-release-imminent/)_[Cyberpunk 2077](https://www.playstationlifestyle.net/2022/01/31/cyberpunk-2077-ps5-release-imminent/)_ has been spotted on PSN. _Hogwarts Legacy_ is also [reportedly set for a September 2022 release date](https://www.playstationlifestyle.net/2022/01/31/hogwarts-legacy-release-date-september-2022/), according to a new leak.

It became a popular tool for content creators and podcasters, offering lifelike voice cloning without requiring users to sign up for an account.

On January 14, 2022, Voiceverse NFT, a company associated with voice actor Troy Baker, was caught plagiarizing voice lines generated by 15.ai for their marketing campaign. They manipulated AI-generated voices of characters from My Little Pony and falsely claimed them as their own. After 15.ai’s developer exposed this with log files, Voiceverse admitted the plagiarism, blaming their marketing team. The controversy, which coincided with Baker's partnership announcement, led to public backlash due to both the plagiarism and environmental concerns around NFTs. Baker eventually ended his partnership with Voiceverse following the scandal.

In the aftermath of this controversy, 15.ai went offline on September 8, 2022, and despite multiple updates from its Twitter account, it has yet to return as of October 2024. Users are still waiting for its re-launch, although it is unclear if and when the platform will come back.

3.content:
**Short description**
: Real-time text-to-speech tool using artificial intelligence

15.ai[![Image 1](https://handwiki.org/wiki/images/thumb/f/f3/15_ai_logo_transparent.png/250px-15_ai_logo_transparent.png)](https://handwiki.org/wiki/File:15_ai_logo_transparent.png)
Type of site[Artificial intelligence](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Artificial_intelligence "Artificial intelligence"), [speech synthesis](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Speech_synthesis "Speech synthesis"), [machine learning](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Machine_learning "Machine learning"), [deep learning](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Deep_learning "Deep learning")
Available in English
[Founder(s)](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Social:Entrepreneurship "Social:Entrepreneurship")15
Website[15.ai](https://15.ai/)
Commercial No
Registration None
Launched**Initial release**: March 2020; 5 years ago

**Stable release**: v24.2.1 / September 2021; 4 years ago
Current status Under maintenance

**15.ai** is a [non-commercial](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Finance:Non-commercial "Finance:Non-commercial")[freeware](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Freeware "Freeware")[artificial intelligence](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Artificial_intelligence "Artificial intelligence")[web application](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Web_application "Web application") that generates natural emotive high-fidelity[[lower-alpha 1]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-4) text-to-speech voices from an assortment of fictional characters from a variety of media sources.[[4]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-kotaku-5)[[5]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-gameinformer-6)[[6]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-pcgamer-7)[[7]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-rockpapershotgun-8) Developed by a [pseudonymous](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Pseudonym "Pseudonym") MIT researcher under the name **15**, the project uses a combination of audio synthesis algorithms, [speech synthesis](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Speech_synthesis "Speech synthesis") deep neural networks, and [sentiment analysis](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Sentiment_analysis "Sentiment analysis") models to generate and serve emotive character voices faster than real-time, particularly those with a very small amount of trainable data.

Launched in early 2020, 15.ai began as a [proof of concept](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Proof_of_concept "Proof of concept") of the [democratization](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Engineering:Democratization_of_technology "Engineering:Democratization of technology") of voice acting and dubbing using technology.[[8]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-thebatch-9) Its gratis and non-commercial nature (with the only stipulation being that the project be properly credited when used), ease of use, no user account registration requirement, and substantial improvements to current text-to-speech implementations have been lauded by users;[[5]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-gameinformer-6)[[9]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-towardds-10)[[4]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-kotaku-5)[[6]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-pcgamer-7) however, some critics and voice actors have questioned the legality and [ethicality](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Philosophy:Ethics_of_artificial_intelligence "Philosophy:Ethics of artificial intelligence") of leaving such technology publicly available and readily accessible.[[8]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-thebatch-9)[[10]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-batch-11)[[11]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-wccftech-12)

Credited as the impetus behind the popularization of AI [voice cloning](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Audio_deepfake "Audio deepfake") (also known as _audio deepfakes_) in [content creation](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Social:Content_creation "Social:Content creation") and as the first publicly available AI vocal synthesis project to involve the use of existing popular fictional characters, 15.ai has had a significant impact on multiple Internet fandoms, most notably the [_My Little Pony: Friendship Is Magic_](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Social:My_Little_Pony:_Friendship_Is_Magic_fandom "Social:My Little Pony: Friendship Is Magic fandom"), _[Team Fortress 2](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Software:Team\_Fortress\_2 "Software:Team Fortress 2")_, and _[SpongeBob SquarePants](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Social:SpongeBob\_SquarePants "Social:SpongeBob SquarePants")_ fandoms. Furthermore, 15.ai has inspired the use of [4chan](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Social:4chan "Social:4chan")'s **Pony Preservation Project** in other [generative artificial intelligence](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Synthetic_media "Synthetic media") projects.[[12]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-automaton-13)[[13]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-Denfaminicogamer-14)

Several commercial alternatives have spawned with the rising popularity of 15.ai, leading to cases of misattribution and theft. In January 2022, it was discovered that **Voiceverse NFT**, a company that voice actor Troy Baker announced his partnership with, had [plagiarized](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Social:Plagiarism "Social:Plagiarism") 15.ai's work as part of their platform.[[14]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-nme-15)[[15]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-stevivor-16)[[16]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-techtimes-17)

On September 8, 2022, 15.ai was temporarily taken down in preparation for an upcoming update, a year after its last stable release (v24.2.1). As of February 2024, it is still temporarily offline.[[17]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-18)

Features
--------

[![Image 2](https://handwiki.org/wiki/images/thumb/f/f6/HAL9000.svg/200px-HAL9000.svg.png)](https://handwiki.org/wiki/File:HAL9000.svg)

HAL 9000, known for his sinister robotic voice, is one of the available characters on 15.ai.[[4]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-kotaku-5)

Available characters include GLaDOS and Wheatley from _Portal_, characters from _[Team Fortress 2](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Software:Team\_Fortress\_2 "Software:Team Fortress 2")_, Twilight Sparkle and a number of main, secondary, and supporting characters from _[My Little Pony](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Social:My\_Little\_Pony:\_Friendship\_Is\_Magic "Social:My Little Pony: Friendship Is Magic")_, SpongeBob from _[SpongeBob SquarePants](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Social:SpongeBob\_SquarePants "Social:SpongeBob SquarePants")_, Daria Morgendorffer and Jane Lane from _Daria_, the Tenth Doctor from _Doctor Who_, HAL 9000 from _2001: A Space Odyssey_, the Narrator from _[The Stanley Parable](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Software:The\_Stanley\_Parable "Software:The Stanley Parable")_, the Wii U/3DS/[Switch](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Software:Super_Smash_Bros._Ultimate "Software:Super Smash Bros. Ultimate")[Super Smash Bros.](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Software:Super_Smash_Bros. "Software:Super Smash Bros.") Announcer (formerly), Carl Brutananadilewski from _Aqua Teen Hunger Force_, Steven Universe from _Steven Universe_, Dan from _Dan Vs._, and [Sans](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Social:Sans_(Undertale) "Social:Sans (Undertale)") from _[Undertale](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Software:Undertale "Software:Undertale")_.[[13]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-Denfaminicogamer-14)[[12]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-automaton-13)[[18]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-LaPS4-19)[[19]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-yahoofin-20)

The [deep learning](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Deep_learning "Deep learning") model used by the application is [nondeterministic](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Nondeterministic_algorithm "Nondeterministic algorithm"): each time that speech is generated from the same string of text, the intonation of the speech will be slightly different. The application also supports manually altering the emotion of a generated line using _emotional contextualizers_ (a term coined by this project), a sentence or phrase that conveys the emotion of the take that serves as a guide for the model during inference.[[9]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-towardds-10)[[12]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-automaton-13)[[13]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-Denfaminicogamer-14) Emotional contextualizers are representations of the emotional content of a sentence deduced via [transfer learned](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Transfer_learning "Transfer learning")[emoji](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Emoji "Emoji")[embeddings](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Word_embedding "Word embedding") using DeepMoji, a deep neural network [sentiment analysis](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Sentiment_analysis "Sentiment analysis") algorithm developed by the [MIT Media Lab](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Organization:MIT_Media_Lab "Organization:MIT Media Lab") in 2017.[[20]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-21)[[21]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-22) DeepMoji was trained on 1.2 billion emoji occurrences in [Twitter](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Company:Twitter "Company:Twitter") data from 2013 to 2017, and has been found to outperform human subjects in correctly identifying sarcasm in Tweets and other online modes of communication.[[22]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-23)[[23]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-24)[[24]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-25)

15.ai uses a _multi-speaker model_—hundreds of voices are trained concurrently rather than sequentially, decreasing the required training time and enabling the model to learn and generalize shared emotional context, even for voices with no exposure to such emotional context.[[25]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-arxivmello-26) Consequently, the entire lineup of characters in the application is powered by a single trained model, as opposed to multiple single-speaker models trained on different datasets.[[26]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-arxivmulti-27) The [lexicon](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Social:Lexicon "Social:Lexicon") used by 15.ai has been scraped from a variety of Internet sources, including Oxford Dictionaries, [Wiktionary](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Social:Wiktionary "Social:Wiktionary"), the [CMU Pronouncing Dictionary](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Software:CMU_Pronouncing_Dictionary "Software:CMU Pronouncing Dictionary"), [4chan](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Social:4chan "Social:4chan"), [Reddit](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Company:Reddit "Company:Reddit"), and [Twitter](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Company:Twitter "Company:Twitter"). Pronunciations of unfamiliar words are automatically deduced using phonological rules learned by the deep learning model.[[12]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-automaton-13)

The application supports a simplified version of a set of English phonetic transcriptions known as ARPABET to correct mispronunciations or to account for heteronyms—words that are spelled the same but are pronounced differently (such as the word _read_, which can be pronounced as either or depending on its [tense](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Social:Grammatical_tense "Social:Grammatical tense")). While the original ARPABET codes developed in the 1970s by the Advanced Research Projects Agency supports 50 unique symbols to designate and differentiate between English phonemes,[[27]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-klautau-28) the [CMU Pronouncing Dictionary](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Software:CMU_Pronouncing_Dictionary "Software:CMU Pronouncing Dictionary")'s ARPABET convention (the set of transcription codes followed by 15.ai[[12]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-automaton-13)) reduces the symbol set to 39 phonemes by combining allophonic phonetic realizations into a single standard (e.g. `AXR/ER`; `UX/UW`) and using multiple common symbols together to replace syllabic consonants (e.g. `EN/AH0 N`).[[28]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-columbia-29)[[29]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-prondicts-30) ARPABET strings can be invoked in the application by wrapping the string of phonemes in curly braces within the input box (e.g. `{AA1 R P AH0 B EH2 T}` to denote , the pronunciation of the word _ARPABET_).[[12]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-automaton-13)

Background
----------

### Speech synthesis

_Main page: [Deep learning speech synthesis](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Deep\_learning\_speech\_synthesis "Deep learning speech synthesis")_[![Image 3](https://handwiki.org/wiki/images/thumb/8/8b/WaveNet_animation.gif/250px-WaveNet_animation.gif)](https://handwiki.org/wiki/File:WaveNet_animation.gif)

A stack of dilated casual convolutional layers used in DeepMind's [WaveNet](https://handwiki.org/wiki/WaveNet "WaveNet").[[3]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-deepmind-3)

In 2016, with the proposal of [DeepMind](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Company:DeepMind "Company:DeepMind")'s [WaveNet](https://handwiki.org/wiki/WaveNet "WaveNet"), deep-learning-based models for speech synthesis began to gain popularity as a method of modeling waveforms and generating human-like speech.[[31]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-arxiv1-32)[[32]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-arxiv2-33)[[3]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-deepmind-3)[[8]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-thebatch-9) Tacotron2, a neural network architecture for speech synthesis developed by [Google AI](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Company:Google_AI "Company:Google AI"), was published in 2018 and required tens of hours of audio data to produce intelligible speech; when trained on 2 hours of speech, the model was able to produce intelligible speech with mediocre quality, and when trained on 36 minutes of speech, the model was unable to produce intelligible speech.[[33]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-tacotron-34)[[34]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-arxiv3-35)

For years, reducing the amount of data required to train a realistic high-quality text-to-speech model has been a primary goal of scientific researchers in the field of deep learning speech synthesis.[[35]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-36)[[36]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-37) The developer of 15.ai claims that as little as 15 seconds of data is sufficient to clone a voice up to human standards, a significant reduction in the amount of data required.[[9]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-towardds-10)[[37]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-eurogamer-38)

### Copyrighted material in deep learning

A landmark case between [Google](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Company:Google "Company:Google") and the Authors Guild in 2013 ruled that [Google Books](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Google_Books "Google Books")—a service that searches the full text of printed copyrighted books—was transformative, thus meeting all requirements for fair use.[[38]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-39) This case set an important legal precedent for the field of deep learning and artificial intelligence: using copyrighted material to train a [discriminative model](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Discriminative_model "Discriminative model") or a _non-commercial_[generative model](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Generative_model "Generative model") was deemed legal.[[39]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-tds-40) The legality of _commercial_ generative models trained using copyrighted material is still under debate; due to the black-box nature of machine learning models, any allegations of copyright infringement via direct competition would be difficult to prove.[[39]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-tds-40)

Development
-----------

15.ai was designed and created by an anonymous research scientist affiliated with the [Massachusetts Institute of Technology](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Organization:Massachusetts_Institute_of_Technology "Organization:Massachusetts Institute of Technology") known by the alias _15_.[[40]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-twitter-41) The project began development while the developer was an undergraduate. The developer has stated that they are capable of paying the high cost of running the site out of pocket.[[9]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-towardds-10)

According to posts made by its developer on [Hacker News](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Social:Hacker_News "Social:Hacker News"), 15.ai costs several thousands of dollars per month to operate; they are able to support the project due to a successful startup [exit](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Social:Exit_strategy "Social:Exit strategy").[[41]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-hn-42) The developer has stated that during their undergraduate years at MIT, they were paid the minimum hourly rate to work on a related project (approximately $14 an hour in [_Massachusetts_](https://www.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts)[[42]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-43)) that eventually evolved into 15.ai. They also stated that the democratization of voice cloning technology is not the only function of the website; in response to a user asking whether the research could be conducted without a public website, the developer wrote:

> [...] The website has multiple purposes. It serves as a [proof of concept](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Proof_of_concept "Proof of concept") of a platform that allows anyone to create content, even if they can't hire someone to voice their projects.
> 
> 
> It also demonstrates the progress of my research in a far more engaging manner—by being able to use the actual model, you can discover things about it that even I wasn't aware of (such as getting characters to make gasping noises or moans by placing commas in between certain phonemes).
> 
> 
> It also doesn't let me get away with [picking and choosing the best results](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Cherry_picking "Cherry picking") and [showing off only the ones that work](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Philosophy:One-sided_argument "Philosophy:One-sided argument") (which I believe is a big problem endemic in [ML](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Machine_learning "Machine learning") today—it's disingenuous and misleading). Being able to interact with the model with no filter allows the user to judge exactly how good the current work is at face value.

The algorithm used by the project to facilitate the cloning of voices with minimal viable data has been dubbed **DeepThroat**[[43]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-15aiabout-44) (a [double entendre](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Double_entendre "Double entendre") in reference to [speech synthesis](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Speech_synthesis "Speech synthesis") using deep neural networks and the sexual act of [deep-throating](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Medicine:Deep-throating "Medicine:Deep-throating")). The project and algorithm—initially conceived as part of MIT's [Undergraduate Research Opportunities Program](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Undergraduate_Research_Opportunities_Program "Undergraduate Research Opportunities Program")—had been in development for years before the first release of the application.[[9]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-towardds-10)[[12]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-automaton-13)

[![Image 4](https://handwiki.org/wiki/images/thumb/0/0f/4chan_Logo.png/250px-4chan_Logo.png)](https://handwiki.org/wiki/File:4chan_Logo.png)

The _Pony Preservation Project_ from 4chan's /mlp/ board has been integral to the development of 15.ai.[[44]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-gwern-45)

The developer has also worked closely with the Pony Preservation Project from /mlp/, the _[My Little Pony](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Social:My\_Little\_Pony:\_Friendship\_Is\_Magic "Social:My Little Pony: Friendship Is Magic")_ board of [4chan](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Social:4chan "Social:4chan"). The **Pony Preservation Project**, which began in 2019, is a "collaborative effort by /mlp/ to build and curate pony datasets" with the aim of creating applications in artificial intelligence.[[44]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-gwern-45)[[45]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-46)[[46]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-ppp-47) The _Friendship Is Magic_ voices on 15.ai were trained on a large dataset crowdsourced by the Pony Preservation Project: audio and dialogue from the show and related media—including all nine seasons of _Friendship Is Magic_, the 2017 movie, spinoffs, [leaks](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Data_breach "Data breach"), and various other content voiced by the same voice actors—were [parsed](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Audio_signal_processing "Audio signal processing"), hand-transcribed, and [processed](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Noise_reduction "Noise reduction") to remove background noise. According to the developer, the collective efforts and constructive criticism from the Pony Preservation Project have been integral to the development of 15.ai.[[44]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-gwern-45)

In addition, the developer has stated that the logo of 15.ai, which features a robotic Twilight Sparkle, is an homage to the fact that her voice (as originally portrayed by Tara Strong) was indispensable to the implementation of emotional contextualizers.[[41]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-hn-42)

Reception
---------

[![Image 5](https://handwiki.org/wiki/images/thumb/a/a3/Andrew_Ng_WSJ_%282%29.jpg/170px-Andrew_Ng_WSJ_%282%29.jpg)](https://handwiki.org/wiki/File:Andrew_Ng_WSJ_(2).jpg)

Computer scientist Andrew Ng wrote that the technology behind 15.ai could potentially open up to cases of impersonation and fraud.

15.ai has been met with largely positive reception. Liana Ruppert of _Game Informer_ described 15.ai as "simplistically brilliant."[[5]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-gameinformer-6) Lauren Morton of _Rock, Paper, Shotgun_ and Natalia Clayton of _PCGamer_ called it "fascinating,"[[7]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-rockpapershotgun-8)[[6]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-pcgamer-7) and José Villalobos of _LaPS4_ wrote that it "works as easy as it looks."[[18]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-LaPS4-19)[[lower-alpha 2]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-48) Users praised the ability to easily create audio of popular characters that sound believable to those unaware that the voices had been synthesized by artificial intelligence: Zack Zwiezen of _Kotaku_ reported that "[his] girlfriend was convinced it was a new voice line from GLaDOS' voice actor, Ellen McLain,"[[4]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-kotaku-5) while Rionaldi Chandraseta of _Towards Data Science_ wrote that, upon watching a [YouTube](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Company:YouTube "Company:YouTube") video featuring popular character voices generated by 15.ai, "[his] first thought was the video creator used [cameo.com](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Cameo_(website) "Cameo (website)") to pay for new dialogues from the original voice actors" and stated that "the quality of voices done by 15.ai is miles ahead of [its competitors]."[[9]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-towardds-10)

Reception has also been largely acclaimed overseas, especially in [_Japan_](https://www.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan) . Takayuki Furushima of _Den Fami Nico Gamer_ has described 15.ai as "like magic," and Yuki Kurosawa of _Automaton Media_ called it "revolutionary."[[13]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-Denfaminicogamer-14)[[12]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-automaton-13)

Computer scientist and technology entrepreneur [Andrew Ng](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Biography:Andrew_Ng "Biography:Andrew Ng") commented in his newsletter _The Batch_ that the technology behind 15.ai could be "enormously productive" and could "revolutionize the use of [virtual actors](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Virtual_actor "Virtual actor")"; however, he also noted that "synthesizing a human actor's voice without consent is arguably unethical and possibly illegal" and could potentially open up to cases of [impersonation and fraud](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Deepfake#Concerns "Deepfake").[[8]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-thebatch-9)[[10]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-batch-11) In his blog _Marginal Revolution_, [economist](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Social:Economist "Social:Economist") Tyler Cowen deemed 15 one of the "most underrated talents in AI and machine learning."[[47]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-49)

Impact
------

### Fandom content creation

15.ai has been frequently used for [content creation](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Social:Content_creation "Social:Content creation") in various fandoms, including the [_My Little Pony: Friendship Is Magic_ fandom](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Social:My_Little_Pony:_Friendship_Is_Magic_fandom "Social:My Little Pony: Friendship Is Magic fandom"), the _[Team Fortress 2](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Software:Team\_Fortress\_2 "Software:Team Fortress 2")_ fandom, the _Portal_ fandom, and the _[SpongeBob SquarePants](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Social:SpongeBob\_SquarePants "Social:SpongeBob SquarePants")_ fandom. Numerous videos and projects containing speech from 15.ai have gone [viral](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Finance:Viral_video "Finance:Viral video").[[9]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-towardds-10)[[4]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-kotaku-5)[[5]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-gameinformer-6) However, some videos and projects that contain non-15.ai-generated speech have also gone viral, many of which do not properly credit the source(s) of the synthetic speech featured in them. As a consequence, many videos and projects that have been made with other speech synthesis software have been mistaken as being made with 15.ai, and vice versa. Due to this misattribution and absence of proper credit, 15.ai's terms of service has a rule that forbids having 15.ai-and-non-15.ai-generated speech in the same videos and projects.[[48]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-15ai-50)

The _My Little Pony: Friendship Is Magic_ fandom has seen a resurgence in video and musical content creation as a direct result, inspiring a new genre of fan-created content assisted by artificial intelligence. Some fanfiction have been adapted into fully voiced "episodes": _The Tax Breaks_ is a 17-minute long animated video rendition of a fan-written story published in 2014 that uses voices generated from 15.ai with sound effects and audio editing, emulating the episodic style of the early seasons of _Friendship Is Magic_.[[49]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-taxbreaks-51)[[50]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-52)

Viral videos from the _Team Fortress 2_ fandom that feature voices from 15.ai include _Spy is a Furry_ (which has gained over 3 million views on YouTube total across multiple videos[[yt 1]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-53)[[yt 2]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-54)[[yt 3]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-55)) and _The RED Bread Bank_, both of which have inspired [Source Filmmaker](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Software:Source_Filmmaker "Software:Source Filmmaker") animated video renditions.[[12]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-automaton-13) Other fandoms have used voices from 15.ai to produce viral videos. (As of July 2022), the viral video _[Among Us](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Software:Among\_Us "Software:Among Us") Struggles_ (which uses voices from _Friendship Is Magic_) has over 5.5 million views on YouTube;[[yt 4]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-56) YouTubers, TikTokers, and [Twitch](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Company:Twitch_(service) "Company:Twitch (service)") streamers have also used 15.ai for their videos, such as FitMC's video on the history of 2b2t—one of the oldest running _[Minecraft](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Software:Minecraft "Software:Minecraft")_ servers—and datpon3's TikTok video featuring the main characters of _Friendship Is Magic_, which have 1.4 million and 510 thousand views, respectively.[[yt 5]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-57)[[tt 1]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-58)

Some users have created AI [virtual assistants](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Engineering:Virtual_assistant "Engineering:Virtual assistant") using 15.ai and external voice control software. One user on Twitter created their own personal GLaDOS desktop assistant using the voice control system VoiceAttack that is able to boot up applications, utter corresponding random dialogues, and thank the user in response to actions.[[12]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-automaton-13)[[13]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-Denfaminicogamer-14)

### Reactions from voice actors

Some voice actors have publicly decried the use of voice cloning technology. Cited reasons include concerns about [impersonation and fraud](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Deepfake#Concerns "Deepfake"), unauthorized use of an actor's voice in [pornography](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Deepfake_pornography "Deepfake pornography"), and the potential of [AI being used to make voice actors obsolete](https://handwiki.org/wiki/Engineering:Technological_unemployment "Engineering:Technological unemployment").[[8]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-thebatch-9)[[10]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-batch-11)[[11]](https://handwiki.org/wiki/15.ai#cite_note-wccftech-12)
